# Nightingale (n9e)

> Open-source alerting engine for Prometheus, VictoriaMetrics, Elasticsearch, ClickHouse and more. Self-hosted, Apache-2.0, with a built-in AI agent and MCP server.

- [Nightingale (n9e)](https://n9e.github.io/index.md)

## categraf

Nightingale evaluates alerts on data you already have. Categraf is one way to put it there: a single agent covering operating systems, middleware, databases, network gear and Kubernetes, writing over Prometheus Remote Write. MIT licensed, built by the team behind Nightingale.

- [Categraf](https://n9e.github.io/categraf.md): Nightingale evaluates alerts on data you already have. Categraf is one way to put it there: a single agent covering operating systems, middleware, databases, network gear and Kubernetes, writing over Prometheus Remote Write. MIT licensed, built by the team behind Nightingale.

## comparisons

Prometheus, Zabbix and Grafana each have their ground. Nightingale argues for one thing only: the alerting layer should belong to a tool built for it.

- [Keep your storage. Change who owns alerting.](https://n9e.github.io/comparisons.md): Prometheus, Zabbix and Grafana each have their ground. Nightingale argues for one thing only: the alerting layer should belong to a tool built for it.

## docs

Start here. Find the task you are trying to finish — connecting a data source, writing a rule, cutting noise, delivering to on-call, deploying to production, or wiring up MCP.

- [Nightingale docs](https://n9e.github.io/docs.md): Start here. Find the task you are trying to finish — connecting a data source, writing a rule, cutting noise, delivering to on-call, deploying to production, or wiring up MCP.

### agent

- [Connect Datadog Agent](https://n9e.github.io/docs/agent/datadog-agent.md): Send Datadog Agent v1 metric series to Nightingale, with the API-version and authentication boundaries made explicit.
- [Connect Telegraf](https://n9e.github.io/docs/agent/telegraf.md): Send Telegraf metrics to Nightingale with HTTP output and Prometheus Remote Write, then verify the stored data.

### ai

- [A2A endpoint](https://n9e.github.io/docs/ai/a2a.md): The A2A endpoint exposes Nightingale as an agent that other agent platforms can discover and call; the agent card declares the address and supported methods.
- [Agents and conversation history](https://n9e.github.io/docs/ai/agents.md): Conversation history is stored server-side and can be reviewed or deleted; in the open-source build an agent is an internal binding, not something you create.
- [Safe automation patterns](https://n9e.github.io/docs/ai/automation.md): Safe AI automation keeps a person in the loop at write time: the assistant proposes and you confirm, one account can write, or AI drafts a script that a human runs.
- [Configure an LLM provider](https://n9e.github.io/docs/ai/llm-provider.md): Point Nightingale at OpenAI-compatible, Anthropic or self-hosted models; keys, base URLs and model selection.
- [Connect Claude Code / Cursor / other clients](https://n9e.github.io/docs/ai/mcp-clients.md): Claude Code, Cursor and other MCP clients connect with just the /mcp URL and a token; one read-only prompt confirms the connection works.
- [Enable the MCP endpoint](https://n9e.github.io/docs/ai/mcp-endpoint.md): The /mcp endpoint is built into the n9e process and on by default; list its tools with curl to confirm it is up, and restrict which toolsets it exposes in config.
- [Nightingale AI overview](https://n9e.github.io/docs/ai/nightingale-ai.md): Nightingale AI is the built-in assistant: it answers questions about alerts, metrics and configuration, drafts changes, and sees only what the asking user can see.
- [OAuth 2.1 and external identity providers](https://n9e.github.io/docs/ai/oauth.md): Nightingale as authorization server for hosted clients, or as resource server in front of Keycloak, Entra ID or Okta.
- [AI and MCP](https://n9e.github.io/docs/ai/overview.md): The built-in assistant, the Skills marketplace, and an MCP endpoint that lets Claude Code or Cursor drive Nightingale with exactly your permissions.
- [Permission inheritance and RBAC](https://n9e.github.io/docs/ai/permissions.md): Every MCP tool call is an internal API call made as the token's user, so a client never sees or changes more than that user; business groups apply unchanged.
- [Install, manage and write Skills](https://n9e.github.io/docs/ai/skills.md): A skill is a procedure in a SKILL.md file: install one from the marketplace or write your own, scope it to teams, and the assistant uses it for matching questions.
- [Personal token authentication](https://n9e.github.io/docs/ai/token-auth.md): Create a token, pass it in X-User-Token, and understand that the client inherits exactly that user's permissions.
- [Read and write toolsets](https://n9e.github.io/docs/ai/toolsets.md): The MCP endpoint offers 74 tools in 13 toolsets; six toolsets are entirely read-only, there are no delete tools, and write tools must be enabled separately.
- [AI / Skill / MCP troubleshooting](https://n9e.github.io/docs/ai/troubleshooting.md): Symptom-by-symptom fixes for the AI features: the assistant stays silent or stops halfway, a skill is ignored or fails to install, an MCP client cannot connect.
- [Common investigation workflows](https://n9e.github.io/docs/ai/workflows.md): Paste-ready investigation prompts paired with the built-in skill that answers each: triage active events, find the noisiest rule, explain a metric spike.
- [Enable write tools safely](https://n9e.github.io/docs/ai/write-tools.md): MCP write tools are not registered by default; enable them explicitly under [HTTP.A2A], scope them to one token, and every change is traceable in the log.

### alerting

- [Rule design best practices](https://n9e.github.io/docs/alerting/best-practices.md): Opinions on rule design: alert only on what needs a person, leave trends to dashboards, size a rule to one class of object, and review so the rule set does not rot.
- [Evaluation interval and recovery](https://n9e.github.io/docs/alerting/evaluation.md): Four timing fields on a rule — interval, for-duration, observation window, recovery — decide when an event is created, when it recovers and when it re-notifies.
- [Inspect evaluation execution records](https://n9e.github.io/docs/alerting/execution-records.md): Every evaluation leaves a record: see what the query returned and why an event did or did not fire.
- [Create the first rule](https://n9e.github.io/docs/alerting/first-rule.md): A rule from scratch: pick the source, write the query, set severity, test fire it, and watch the event appear.
- [Import, export and reuse](https://n9e.github.io/docs/alerting/import-export.md): Move rules between environments as JSON, and keep them in version control.
- [Labels, annotations and severity](https://n9e.github.io/docs/alerting/labels-severity.md): Attach labels for routing, write annotations that read well in a notification, and choose S1 / S2 / S3 deliberately.
- [Log rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/alerting/log-rules.md): Alert on log counts or matched patterns from ElasticSearch, OpenSearch, Loki and VictoriaLogs — all four alert, but only three can be previewed in the Log explorer.
- [Metric rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/alerting/metric-rules.md): Metric rules put the threshold inside the PromQL expression; one rule can carry several severities, and the labels the query returns land on the event for routing.
- [Alert rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/alerting/overview.md): Rules are configured in the UI, scoped by business group, graded S1 / S2 / S3, and can span several data sources. A library of common rules ships with the install.
- [Scope by business group and data source](https://n9e.github.io/docs/alerting/scope.md): A rule has two scopes: the business group decides who may edit it and owns its events; the data source list decides which instances it queries, and can span several.
- [SQL-backed rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/alerting/sql-rules.md): Rules that run a SQL statement against MySQL, PostgreSQL, ClickHouse, Doris, TDengine or IoTDB on a schedule.
- [Rule templates and built-in rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/alerting/templates.md): Nightingale ships rule templates for MySQL, Redis, Kubernetes and sixty other components; import them into any business group, and save your own rules as templates.
- [Test fire a rule](https://n9e.github.io/docs/alerting/test-fire.md): Fire a rule on demand to check the query, labels and the rendered notification before it goes live.

### concepts

The mental model behind the product: which processes exist, how a data source becomes an alert, and how events are thinned out on their way to a person.

- [Architecture and concepts](https://n9e.github.io/docs/concepts.md): The mental model behind the product: which processes exist, how a data source becomes an alert, and how events are thinned out on their way to a person.
- [Alert lifecycle and S1 / S2 / S3 severity](https://n9e.github.io/docs/concepts/alert-lifecycle.md): An event is identified by rule plus label set and passes through firing, ongoing and recovered; S1 / S2 / S3 change nothing mechanically — they signal urgency.
- [System architecture](https://n9e.github.io/docs/concepts/architecture.md): The core is one n9e process: no dependencies for testing, MySQL and Redis for production, several instances sharing them for a cluster, and n9e-edge for multi-site.
- [Authentication, tokens and RBAC model](https://n9e.github.io/docs/concepts/auth-rbac.md): Two layers: roles decide which pages and endpoints are reachable, business-group membership decides which data can be touched; UI, HTTP API and MCP share the model.
- [Business groups and resource ownership](https://n9e.github.io/docs/concepts/business-groups.md): Business groups are the permission boundary: every rule, target and dashboard belongs to one, and membership decides who can see or change it.
- [Center, Alert, Edge, Pushgw and Categraf](https://n9e.github.io/docs/concepts/components.md): Most deployments need only the n9e process; n9e-alert and n9e-pushgw are roles that can be split out, n9e-edge serves multi-site setups, Categraf collects on hosts.
- [Datasource → rule → event model](https://n9e.github.io/docs/concepts/data-model.md): The three objects everything else hangs off: a data source is queried by a rule, and a rule that trips produces an event.
- [Evaluation, recovery and state changes](https://n9e.github.io/docs/concepts/evaluation.md): A rule does not fire on the first high value: three timing parameters and a small state machine decide when it first fires, when it recovers and whether it flaps.
- [Labels, annotations and identity](https://n9e.github.io/docs/concepts/labels-annotations.md): Labels decide which event this is; annotations decide what the notification says. They are not interchangeable.
- [Noise reduction and routing model](https://n9e.github.io/docs/concepts/noise-routing.md): Mute rules, subscriptions, pipelines and notification rules are not alternatives: they act on an event in a fixed order, which is why a muted alert can still page.
- [Embedded TSDB and external storage](https://n9e.github.io/docs/concepts/storage.md): Nightingale ships with an embedded TSDB for onboarding; this page explains its limits and when to switch to Prometheus or VictoriaMetrics.

### data

- [Categraf](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/categraf.md): The recommended collector: one agent, 100+ input plugins, pushing over Prometheus Remote Write.
- [Install and register](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/categraf/install.md): Install the agent, set the Nightingale write URL, and confirm the host shows up under Targets.
- [Input plugins](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/categraf/plugins.md): Categraf ships over ninety input plugins; a config file in conf/input.<name> enables one, and a single plugin can run alone in the foreground for testing.
- [Remote write](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/categraf/remote-write.md): Categraf batches metrics and ships them over Prometheus Remote Write; several writers can feed Nightingale and a second backend at once; failed writes are not retried.
- [Targets and heartbeat](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/categraf/targets.md): Categraf sends a heartbeat with host metadata every ten seconds; the target list shows status and tags from it, and hosts are assigned to business groups by hand.
- [Troubleshooting](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/categraf/troubleshooting.md): Categraf problems come in three symptoms — host missing, host present but no metrics, one plugin silent — and the log has the answer, even for errors not marked E!.
- [ClickHouse / Doris / IoTDB](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/clickhouse-doris-iotdb.md): ClickHouse, Doris and IoTDB are one family in Nightingale: queried with SQL, one numeric column of the result becomes the series value and the rest become labels.
- [ElasticSearch / OpenSearch](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/elasticsearch.md): Connect an ES or OpenSearch cluster, choose index patterns and the timestamp field, and run a log query.
- [Auto-registered Embedded TSDB datasource](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/embedded-tsdb.md): A fresh install auto-registers a Prometheus-type source named embedded-tsdb; Pushgw writes into it by default, and it is queried like any external Prometheus source.
- [Integration templates](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations.md): 86 templates that bundle collector config, dashboards and alert rules so a component is onboarded as a set.
- [Install collector configuration](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/collector-config.md): Copy a template's collector config into Categraf and start collecting the component's metrics.
- [Import dashboards and rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/import.md): Import the bundled dashboards and alert rules into a business group, and adjust thresholds before enabling.
- [Verify incoming data](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/integrations/verify.md): A quiet imported rule may just mean no data arrived; query the metric name the template lists in the Metrics explorer to confirm the component's metrics are in.
- [Loki / VictoriaLogs](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/loki-victorialogs.md): Register a log store, write a LogQL or LogsQL query, and alert on counts or matches.
- [Connect your data](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/overview.md): Nightingale queries your stores where they are. Twelve source types share one rule model; Categraf covers what nothing collects yet.
- [Prometheus](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/prometheus.md): Register a Prometheus or Thanos endpoint, set auth and timeouts, and verify with a query.
- [MySQL / PostgreSQL / TDengine](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/sql-databases.md): Alert on a business database directly: read-only credentials, the SQL a rule runs, and guarding against slow queries.
- [VictoriaMetrics](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/victoriametrics.md): There is no separate VictoriaMetrics type: register it as Prometheus and set the TSDB type to VictoriaMetrics; single-node and cluster endpoints differ.

### events

- [Active and historical events](https://n9e.github.io/docs/events/active-historical.md): Active events hold alerts that have not recovered; on recovery they move to history. Both lists are searchable by label, severity and business group, in bulk.
- [Event aggregation and deduplication](https://n9e.github.io/docs/events/aggregation.md): One rule plus one label set is one event, so repeated evaluations never create a second; the aggregation view folds hundreds of active events into a few cards.
- [AI summary processor](https://n9e.github.io/docs/events/ai-summary.md): Have an LLM write a short summary onto each event before it is notified: model setup, the prompt template, where the result lands, and what happens when the call fails.
- [Inspect workflow execution records](https://n9e.github.io/docs/events/execution-records.md): Execution records trace each event through every processor: what each one changed, whether the event was dropped, and where it was sent.
- [Mute rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/events/mute-rules.md): Silence by label match, time window or maintenance schedule, and see what a mute rule is currently swallowing.
- [Noise reduction patterns](https://n9e.github.io/docs/events/noise-patterns.md): Recipes that hold up in production: flapping, storms during deploys, duplicate sources, and what should never page a human.
- [Events, noise reduction and routing](https://n9e.github.io/docs/events/overview.md): What happens to an event between the rule that fired it and the person who receives it — mute rules, subscriptions, event pipelines, and self-healing.
- [Event pipelines](https://n9e.github.io/docs/events/pipelines.md): Ordered processors that transform, enrich, drop or route an event before notification.
- [Rewrite labels and enrich context](https://n9e.github.io/docs/events/relabel-enrich.md): Rename or add labels, or call your own service and write what it returns back onto the event.
- [Conditional routing](https://n9e.github.io/docs/events/routing.md): Send an event to different channels or teams depending on its labels and severity.
- [Trigger self-healing with ibex / webhook](https://n9e.github.io/docs/events/self-healing.md): Run a script on the affected host through ibex, or call a webhook, when a specific event fires.
- [Alert subscriptions](https://n9e.github.io/docs/events/subscriptions.md): Let a team receive events from rules they do not own, with their own channel and severity filter.
- [Try a workflow with a mock event](https://n9e.github.io/docs/events/try-workflow.md): Run a pipeline against a hand-written event and see each processor's output before anything is live.

### get-started

- [Choose your path](https://n9e.github.io/docs/get-started/choose-your-path.md): Four starting points depending on what you already run. Each one ends with a rule evaluating real data.
- [I need to monitor a host with Categraf](https://n9e.github.io/docs/get-started/choose-your-path/categraf.md): Install Categraf on a host, point it at Nightingale over Remote Write, and see the machine appear under Targets within a minute.
- [I already have logs or databases](https://n9e.github.io/docs/get-started/choose-your-path/existing-logs-databases.md): Alert on ElasticSearch, Loki, ClickHouse, MySQL and the other SQL-queried stores using the same rule model as metrics.
- [I already have Prometheus / VictoriaMetrics](https://n9e.github.io/docs/get-started/choose-your-path/existing-metrics.md): Register the store as a data source, keep scraping exactly as before, and get the first rule evaluating against it — no data moves.
- [I want to enable Nightingale AI](https://n9e.github.io/docs/get-started/choose-your-path/nightingale-ai.md): Configure an LLM provider, turn on the built-in assistant and the MCP endpoint, and connect a client such as Claude Code.
- [What Nightingale (n9e) is](https://n9e.github.io/docs/get-started/introduction.md): Nightingale (n9e, 夜莺) is an open-source alerting engine: it evaluates rules on the stores you already run, cuts the noise and delivers to on-call; it stores and collects nothing.
- [Guided live demo](https://n9e.github.io/docs/get-started/live-demo.md): Sign in to the public demo and walk the path from data source to delivered alert, in the same order as the quick start — no install needed.
- [Production readiness checklist](https://n9e.github.io/docs/get-started/production-checklist.md): What to change before real traffic: default credentials, external database, TSDB choice, HA, backups and self-monitoring.
- [Bring up Nightingale in five minutes](https://n9e.github.io/docs/get-started/quick-start.md): One docker compose up -d brings up Nightingale with its dependencies; sign in on port 17000 as root, then register a data source, write a rule and add a channel.
- [Where it fits in the observability stack](https://n9e.github.io/docs/get-started/where-it-fits.md): Of the six observability layers, Nightingale owns the middle three — rules, noise reduction, routing and delivery; collectors, storage and Grafana stay as they are.

### help

- [Deprecations and EOL policy](https://n9e.github.io/docs/help/deprecations.md): Features, fields and UI items marked deprecated, with their replacements; the project publishes no removal schedule, and GitHub releases are the version record.
- [Release notes](https://n9e.github.io/docs/help/release-notes.md): Curated notes per release with upgrade impact, in addition to the GitHub changelog.

### install

- [Binary packages](https://n9e.github.io/docs/install/binary.md): Download the Linux amd64 / arm64 tarball from GitHub releases, verify the checksum, point it at your MySQL and Redis, and run n9e under systemd.
- [Configuration layout](https://n9e.github.io/docs/install/configuration.md): Configuration is a directory: config.toml is read by n9e, alert and pushgw, etc/edge by n9e-edge; environment variables fill in blanks but never override set keys.
- [MySQL / PostgreSQL / SQLite and Redis](https://n9e.github.io/docs/install/databases.md): The metadata store is MySQL, PostgreSQL or SQLite (testing only); the process creates the schema on first start, and Redis holds runtime state such as heartbeats.
- [Docker Compose](https://n9e.github.io/docs/install/docker-compose.md): Bring up Nightingale with its database and time-series store in one command; what the bundle contains and how to change it.
- [Edge data centers](https://n9e.github.io/docs/install/edge.md): A local alerting engine for sites whose link to the center is unreliable, and the one flag that silently breaks it.
- [Embedded TSDB for onboarding and small scale](https://n9e.github.io/docs/install/embedded-tsdb.md): Use the built-in store to get going with zero extra components; retention, capacity and the single-Center constraint.
- [External TSDB and dual-write migration](https://n9e.github.io/docs/install/external-tsdb.md): Move from the embedded store to Prometheus or VictoriaMetrics without a gap, using Pushgw dual write.
- [Helm / Kubernetes](https://n9e.github.io/docs/install/helm.md): A community-maintained Helm chart deploys Nightingale on Kubernetes with MySQL, Redis, Prometheus and Categraf; values can point it at databases outside the cluster.
- [High availability](https://n9e.github.io/docs/install/high-availability.md): Run multiple Center and Alert instances behind a load balancer, and what still needs to be a singleton.
- [Offline deployment](https://n9e.github.io/docs/install/offline.md): Install on hosts without internet access: packages, images and integration templates to fetch in advance.
- [Installation and deployment](https://n9e.github.io/docs/install/overview.md): The ways to run Nightingale — Compose, Docker image, binaries, Helm, n9e-edge — and which fits which situation.
- [Rollback](https://n9e.github.io/docs/install/rollback.md): Return to the previous version after a failed upgrade, including what to do about schema migrations that already ran.
- [Uninstall and data retention](https://n9e.github.io/docs/install/uninstall.md): Remove Nightingale cleanly, and what to keep or export before you do.
- [Upgrade](https://n9e.github.io/docs/install/upgrade.md): Upgrade between minor versions and across v8 → v9: back up first, read the database changes, roll the binaries.

### migration

Coming from another alerting stack, or from Nightingale v8: what maps to what, and how to run both during the switch.

- [Migration and comparison](https://n9e.github.io/docs/migration.md): Coming from another alerting stack, or from Nightingale v8: what maps to what, and how to run both during the switch.
- [Coexistence and rollback plan](https://n9e.github.io/docs/migration/coexistence.md): Run both systems on the same data during the switch, compare what fires, and cut over channel by channel.
- [From Prometheus + Alertmanager](https://n9e.github.io/docs/migration/from-alertmanager.md): Keep Prometheus for storage and scraping; move rules, routes, silences and receivers into Nightingale objects.
- [From Grafana Alerting](https://n9e.github.io/docs/migration/from-grafana-alerting.md): Keep Grafana dashboards; move alert rules and contact points, and what to do about unified alerting state.
- [From Zabbix](https://n9e.github.io/docs/migration/from-zabbix.md): Moving from Zabbix is a rebuild: hosts map to targets, templates to integrations, triggers to rules; some concepts have no equivalent, and Zabbix never has to stop.
- [v8 to v9](https://n9e.github.io/docs/migration/v8-to-v9.md): v8 to v9 is a binary swap with the schema migrated on startup, but several new config sections must be added by hand or the new features stay silently off.

### notifications

- [Notification architecture](https://n9e.github.io/docs/notifications/architecture.md): Three objects carry a notification: the rule picks recipients, the media type says how to send, the template says what to send; a missing link makes it vanish.
- [Callback (generic webhook)](https://n9e.github.io/docs/notifications/callback.md): POST events to any HTTP endpoint: the URL, headers and body template, the variables they can use, and when a call counts as delivered.
- [Slack / Telegram / Discord / Mattermost](https://n9e.github.io/docs/notifications/chat.md): Webhook-based chat channels, and how to format a message that survives each one's markdown.
- [Retries and delivery status](https://n9e.github.io/docs/notifications/delivery.md): Failed sends are retried only for connection failures, with parameters per send type; the outcome of every message is in the notification log, kept for seven days.
- [DingTalk / Feishu / WeCom](https://n9e.github.io/docs/notifications/dingtalk-feishu-wecom.md): Robot webhooks and card messages for the three major Chinese workplace apps.
- [Email / Phone / SMS](https://n9e.github.io/docs/notifications/email-phone-sms.md): SMTP settings, and voice and SMS through Aliyun and Tencent Cloud.
- [PagerDuty / FlashDuty / Jira](https://n9e.github.io/docs/notifications/oncall-ticketing.md): Hand events to an on-call platform or open a ticket, with the field mapping each one expects.
- [Notifications](https://n9e.github.io/docs/notifications/overview.md): How an event reaches a person — media types, message templates and notification rules, and which of them ship configured.
- [Notification rules](https://n9e.github.io/docs/notifications/rules.md): Match events by label and severity, then pick the media type, the template and the recipients.
- [Script media type](https://n9e.github.io/docs/notifications/script.md): Hand events to your own program: how the script is stored and run, what arrives on stdin, and how success and failure are recorded.
- [Templates and variables](https://n9e.github.io/docs/notifications/templates.md): Templates are Go text/template with every variable under $event; a misspelled variable raises no error and just leaves a hole in the message — preview catches it.
- [Test a notification end to end](https://n9e.github.io/docs/notifications/test.md): Send a test message through a real channel, from rule to phone, before you rely on it at 3 a.m.

### operations

Keeping Nightingale itself healthy: topology, capacity, backups, upgrades, and knowing when it is the one that is broken.

- [Operations](https://n9e.github.io/docs/operations.md): Keeping Nightingale itself healthy: topology, capacity, backups, upgrades, and knowing when it is the one that is broken.
- [Backup and restore](https://n9e.github.io/docs/operations/backup-restore.md): Only the metadata database and the etc/ directory are irreplaceable: back both up on a schedule and rehearse the restore; embedded TSDB metrics can be re-collected.
- [Capacity planning](https://n9e.github.io/docs/operations/capacity.md): Load is driven by rule count, series count, event volume and database traffic; measure four numbers to know where to scale — there is deliberately no sizing table.
- [Logs and diagnostic bundles](https://n9e.github.io/docs/operations/diagnostics.md): Four sources when Nightingale itself misbehaves: the process log, evaluation records, /metrics and pprof — collect all four before opening an issue.
- [Disaster recovery](https://n9e.github.io/docs/operations/disaster-recovery.md): Rebuild from backups in a new environment, and the order in which to bring components back.
- [Edge network partition behavior](https://n9e.github.io/docs/operations/edge-partition.md): What n9e-edge does when it loses the center: evaluation continues, notifications go local, and what syncs back later.
- [Embedded TSDB single-Center limits](https://n9e.github.io/docs/operations/embedded-tsdb-limits.md): The embedded store lives inside one Center process: what that rules out and when to move off it.
- [Built-in metrics and health checks](https://n9e.github.io/docs/operations/health.md): The /metrics and health endpoints each process exposes, and the handful worth graphing.
- [High availability and failure domains](https://n9e.github.io/docs/operations/high-availability.md): Which failures a multi-instance deployment survives, which it does not, and how to test it.
- [Pushgw queue, writers and dual write](https://n9e.github.io/docs/operations/pushgw.md): The write path: queue sizing, backpressure, multiple writers and forwarding to two backends.
- [Rollback and recovery](https://n9e.github.io/docs/operations/rollback.md): Undo an upgrade or a bad config push, and recover from a corrupted metadata database.
- [Monitor Nightingale itself](https://n9e.github.io/docs/operations/self-monitoring.md): Rules that page you when the alerting system is the thing that is down.
- [Production topology](https://n9e.github.io/docs/operations/topology.md): Reference layouts for one team, one company, and multi-site with edge alerting.
- [Upgrade and database migration](https://n9e.github.io/docs/operations/upgrade.md): How schema migrations run on startup, and how to upgrade a multi-instance deployment in order.

### troubleshooting

Organised by symptom, not by component: find the line that matches what you are seeing.

- [Troubleshooting](https://n9e.github.io/docs/troubleshooting.md): Organised by symptom, not by component: find the line that matches what you are seeing.
- [Alert fires repeatedly or never recovers](https://n9e.github.io/docs/troubleshooting/alert-flapping.md): Flapping or never-recovering alerts usually come from a threshold sitting on the data, a data gap read as recovery, a changing label set, or no recovery condition.
- [Query works but the alert does not fire](https://n9e.github.io/docs/troubleshooting/alert-not-firing.md): Query has data but nothing fires: the evaluation records hold the answer — for-duration not met, wrong datasource_queries, group or window mismatch, disabled, muted.
- [Categraf target is offline](https://n9e.github.io/docs/troubleshooting/categraf-offline.md): A target shows offline when its heartbeat has not reached Redis in time — clock skew, a wrong heartbeat URL or network policy; update time is not a liveness signal.
- [Edge loses contact with the center](https://n9e.github.io/docs/troubleshooting/edge-disconnected.md): During a partition the edge keeps alerting locally but its events never reach the center — that is expected; an edge that never connected is a misconfiguration.
- [Embedded TSDB has fragmented or missing data](https://n9e.github.io/docs/troubleshooting/embedded-tsdb-data.md): Gaps in the embedded TSDB rarely raise errors — retention, disk pressure or restarts; three timestamp metrics show whether the gap is on the write or the query side.
- [Evaluation records are missing or dropped](https://n9e.github.io/docs/troubleshooting/evaluation-missing.md): Missing evaluation records mean one of four things: not recorded, not evaluated, query rejected or cycle skipped; overload and datasource timeouts are the usual causes.
- [MCP authentication fails](https://n9e.github.io/docs/troubleshooting/mcp-auth.md): MCP authentication fails at the gateway, the token check or OAuth — the status code says which; usual causes: wrong header name, expired token, bad redirect URL.
- [MCP tools are missing or denied](https://n9e.github.io/docs/troubleshooting/mcp-tools-missing.md): "No such tool" has three shapes — write tools not enabled, toolset disabled, or the token's user lacks the permission — and the tools/list response tells them apart.
- [Data source connects but queries return no data](https://n9e.github.io/docs/troubleshooting/no-data.md): A source passes its test but returns nothing: check write, store and query in turn — nothing written, time range past the last point, label mismatch, wrong store.
- [Alert event exists but no notification arrives](https://n9e.github.io/docs/troubleshooting/no-notification.md): Event but no message: in the notification log, no record means a mute or notification rule stopped it; a failure points at the channel, a success at the receiver.
- [Performance and backlog symptoms](https://n9e.github.io/docs/troubleshooting/performance.md): Late alerts, growing queues and high database CPU each map to one built-in metric that localises the cause; pick the metric by symptom, then work back to the root.
- [Notification template rendering fails](https://n9e.github.io/docs/troubleshooting/template-errors.md): A message body that is error text, or a field that is empty, is a template rendering problem that still logs as success; preview against a real event to catch it.
- [Upgrade or database migration fails](https://n9e.github.io/docs/troubleshooting/upgrade-fails.md): Unknown column errors, blank pages or a hung process after an upgrade mean the schema did not fully migrate — usually missing database privileges or an interrupted run.
- [Workflow Try run succeeds but production execution fails](https://n9e.github.io/docs/troubleshooting/workflow-prod-fails.md): Try run passes, production fails: real events may lack labels the mock had, and the alert process — not the UI — runs the workflow with its own permissions and network.
- [Event pipeline routes to the wrong destination](https://n9e.github.io/docs/troubleshooting/wrong-routing.md): Wrong recipients usually mean the destination was decided earlier than expected: processor order, a label rewrite before the match, or the two mount points' scopes.

# Categraf

Nightingale evaluates alerts on data you already have. Categraf is one way to put it there: a single agent covering operating systems, middleware, databases, network gear and Kubernetes, writing over Prometheus Remote Write. MIT licensed, built by the team behind Nightingale.

100+Collection plugins

MITLicensed

1Agent per host

## Install and run

### Download a release build

Archives are per platform and already contain the conf directory, so the agent runs straight out of the tarball. Linux ships for amd64 and arm64, Windows as a zip. Two variants sit beside the default build: -with-cgo-plugin adds the NVIDIA DCGM collector, and categraf-slim drops everything but metrics collection.

`tar xzf categraf-v<version>-linux-amd64.tar.gzcd categraf-v<version>-linux-amd64`

The version is part of the filename, so there is no fixed “latest” URL — pick the build from the releases page.

[Releases on GitHub](https://github.com/flashcatcloud/categraf/releases)

<!-- -->

[ →](https://github.com/flashcatcloud/categraf/releases)

### Docker

The image carries the binary at /usr/bin/categraf and the sample config at /etc/categraf/conf. Set N9E\_HOST and the entrypoint rewrites the server address inside config.toml for you; mount your own conf directory when you need more than that.

`docker pull flashcatcloud/categraf:latestdocker run -d --name categraf -e N9E_HOST=192.168.1.10:17000 flashcatcloud/categraf:latest`

### Build from source

Go 1.25 or newer. Package the binary together with conf so the agent keeps its sample configuration alongside it.

`go buildtar zcvf categraf.tar.gz categraf conf`

On macOS use gnu-tar (gtar) — the bundled bsdtar produces an archive Categraf refuses to load.

### See what it collects before writing anywhere

Test mode prints metrics straight to stdout, so you can confirm a plugin works before pointing the agent at a server.

`./categraf --test./categraf --test --inputs system:mem`

### Run it

Configuration lives in the conf directory — config.toml for the agent itself, one input.\<plugin> directory per collector. Restrict the run to specific plugins with --inputs.

`./categraf./categraf --configs /path/to/conf-directory./categraf --inputs system:mem`

Connecting it to Nightingale, tagging hosts, and what to check when no data arrives are covered step by step in the docs.

[Categraf docs](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/categraf.md)

<!-- -->

[ →](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/categraf.md)

### Kubernetes

A DaemonSet collects node and cAdvisor metrics, a Deployment covers cluster-level targets such as apiserver and CoreDNS, and a sidecar covers one service. The manifests ship in the repository.

`kubectl apply -n monitoring -f k8s/daemonset.yamlkubectl apply -n monitoring -f k8s/deployment.yamlkubectl apply -n monitoring -f k8s/sidecar.yaml`

### Where the data goes

Categraf pushes over the Prometheus Remote Write protocol, so it writes into Nightingale, Prometheus, VictoriaMetrics or anything else that speaks it. Push means the agent opens the connection — which matters when network policy will not let a central server reach into every subnet.

[Register it as a data source](https://n9e.github.io/integrations.md)

<!-- -->

[ →](https://n9e.github.io/integrations.md)

### Not the only option

Nightingale does not require Categraf. Telegraf, the Datadog Agent and standard Prometheus exporters write in the same way, and a Prometheus that already scrapes your targets can stay exactly as it is.

[Categraf source and releases](https://github.com/flashcatcloud/categraf)

Nightingale vs[Prometheus + Alertmanager](#prometheus)[Zabbix](#zabbix)[Grafana Alerting](#grafana)

# Keep your storage.<br /><!-- -->Change who owns alerting.

Prometheus, Zabbix and Grafana each have their ground. Nightingale argues for one thing only: the alerting layer should belong to a tool built for it.

[Try live demo](http://43.106.19.165/api/n9e/auth/demo-login)[Install in 5 minutes](https://n9e.github.io/docs/get-started/quick-start.md)

## At a glance

| Capability comparison           | Nightingale v9                                | Prometheus + Alertmanager                               | Zabbix                                                  | Grafana Alerting                                       |
| ------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| Alerting across data sources    | Built in<!-- -->: Metrics and logs, 10+ types | Not available<!-- -->: Prometheus data only             | Not available<!-- -->: Its own collection stack         | Partial or via add-on<!-- -->: Per data source plugin  |
| Notification channels           | Built in<!-- -->: 20 built in, phone and SMS  | Partial or via add-on<!-- -->: Webhooks, build your own | Partial or via add-on<!-- -->: Media types plus scripts | Partial or via add-on<!-- -->: Some built in           |
| Mute, subscribe, event pipeline | Built in<!-- -->: Native                      | Partial or via add-on<!-- -->: Basic silences           | Partial or via add-on<!-- -->: Maintenance windows      | Partial or via add-on<!-- -->: Basic silences          |
| Rules and permissions in the UI | Built in<!-- -->: Business-group RBAC         | Not available<!-- -->: YAML and reload                  | Built in<!-- -->: Yes                                   | Built in<!-- -->: Yes                                  |
| Built-in AI and MCP server      | Built in<!-- -->: 74 tools, in-process        | Not available<!-- -->: None                             | Not available<!-- -->: None                             | Partial or via add-on<!-- -->: Assistant is Cloud-only |

* Partial or via add-on

Based on the publicly documented capabilities of each project’s open-source edition as of August 2026. We try to state what the other tools are good at — advice you cannot trust is worth nothing to a community.

* **13,330**GitHub stars
* **10+**&#x44;ata source types
* **20**Notification channels
* **74**MCP tools

## AI is part of the process, not an add-on

It reads your alerts, rules and metrics, so answers come from your data rather than the model’s memory. Before it changes anything that already exists, it shows you the diff.

### 01Investigate

It pulls the event, the rule, runs the rule’s query over the window, checks neighbouring hosts and muting rules, and hands back an evidence chain. The call is still yours.

### 02Cut the noise

Which rules are the noisiest and which have never fired, in one question. For the ones that recur on a schedule, ask whether they are candidates for self-healing.

### 03Change configuration

Changes to existing objects take two turns: the tool returns a confirmation card first and writes only after you confirm. A proposal expires in 30 minutes, applies once, and is refused if someone edited the object meanwhile. There are no delete tools.

Nightingale AI · event #48213

Event #48213 · MySQL replica lag > 30s · mysql-prod

Analyze the root cause of this alert event

Read the event and its ruleget\_alert\_event · get\_alert\_rule

Run the rule’s query over the firing windowquery\_range · 14:00–14:20

Check other alerts on the host and muting rulesops-troubleshooting

✓Lag has stayed above 30s since 14:02. On the same host disk\_io\_util reached 96% at 14:01, and two disk alerts fired in the same window. No muting rule was in play. Three pieces of evidence are listed; whether it is the root cause is your call.

* 74 MCP tools
* 13 toolsets
* No delete tools
* Permissions follow the user
* OpenAI-compatible, Anthropic or self-hosted models
* Claude Code and Cursor connect directly

01

## Prometheus + Alertmanager

Their way

Rules live in YAML and ship through GitOps.

The Nightingale way

Rules live in the UI, scoped by business group.

### Where it shines

Prometheus remains one of the best time-series foundations available, and Alertmanager’s grouping and silencing model is genuinely clean. At moderate scale, with a GitOps-comfortable team and a rule count you can hold in your head, the pair is enough and adds no components.

### When Nightingale fits better

Nightingale earns its place when rules must be maintained by teams who are not SREs, when permissions need to follow business groups, when someone has to be phoned at 3am, or when the data is not all in Prometheus.

### Signs it is time to switch

* Rules must be maintained by teams who are not SREs
* Someone has to be phoned at 3am, not just webhooked
* The data is no longer all in Prometheus

Migration guide[From Prometheus + Alertmanager<!-- --> →](https://n9e.github.io/docs/migration/from-alertmanager.md)

rules.yml + alertmanager.yml

```
- alert: MysqlReplicaLag  expr: mysql_slave_lag_seconds > 30  for: 5m  labels: { team: dba }route:  receiver: dba-webhook  group_by: [alertname]
```

Nightingale · alert rule

* Name

  MySQL replica lag

* Condition

  mysql\_slave\_lag\_seconds > 30, for 5m

* Business group

  DBA

* Notify

  Phone, SMS, DingTalk

* Who can edit

  DBA group

One rule, two ways to write it

* You

  Create in one sentence: page the DBA group by phone when mysql-prod replica lag stays above 30s for 5 minutes

* Nightingale AI

  PromQL and threshold drafted. I will not guess the business group; pick one from the list and I will create the rule.

02

## Zabbix

Their way

Collect everything with its own agents, then alert on that.

The Nightingale way

Alert on the stores you already fill; collect only where nothing does.

### Where it shines

Two decades of work show in traditional IT monitoring: network gear, SNMP, agent-based collection and auto-discovery are its home ground, and the hiring pool knows it well.

### When Nightingale fits better

If your telemetry already lives in Prometheus, VictoriaMetrics or ElasticSearch, Nightingale reads it directly instead of asking you to pour it into a second collection stack.

### Signs it is time to switch

* Telemetry already lives in Prometheus, VictoriaMetrics or ElasticSearch
* Kubernetes and cloud services outnumber network gear
* You maintain two collection stacks to get one alert

Migration guide[From Zabbix<!-- --> →](https://n9e.github.io/docs/migration/from-zabbix.md)

Categraf fills only the gaps

* You

  Why did this host go offline?

* Nightingale AI

  The agent stopped reporting 3 minutes ago, but the host answers ping and its neighbours are healthy. That points to the Categraf process exiting, not the host going down.

03

## Grafana Alerting

Their way

Alerting as a module inside the visualization platform.

The Nightingale way

Alerting as the whole product; chart wherever you like.

### Where it shines

Grafana is the visualization standard and its dashboard ecosystem has no real substitute. If alert volume is modest and Grafana is already in place, its built-in alerting is one system fewer to run.

### When Nightingale fits better

Nightingale puts everything into the alerting side: event pipelines, subscriptions, self-healing. The two are not exclusive — plenty of users chart in Grafana and alert in Nightingale.

### Signs it is time to switch

* Alert volume has outgrown a panel-level rule model
* You need event pipelines, subscriptions or self-healing
* On-call people need phone and SMS, not only contact points

Migration guide[From Grafana Alerting<!-- --> →](https://n9e.github.io/docs/migration/from-grafana-alerting.md)

Grafana · MySQL overview

A Grafana panel embedded by URL in a Nightingale dashboard

S1MySQL replica lag > 30s

`ident=mysql-prod``busigroup=DBA`

Delivered · phone and DingTalk

## Nothing has to be switched off

Nightingale reads the storage you already run, so the switch is a parallel run, not a cut-over.

1. 1

   ### Point it at your storage

   Register Prometheus, VictoriaMetrics or ElasticSearch as a data source. Nothing in the collection path changes.

2. 2

   ### Move the rules across

   The migration guides map every entry of an alertmanager.yml or a Grafana alert rule onto a Nightingale object, and say plainly which ones have no equivalent.

3. 3

   ### Run both, cut over by channel

   Compare what fires each day, switch one notification channel at a time, and back out of any stage in about a minute.

[Coexistence and rollback plan<!-- --> →](https://n9e.github.io/docs/migration/coexistence.md)

## Questions people ask before switching

Can I keep Grafana?

Yes, and it is the most common setup: chart in Grafana, alert in Nightingale. A Nightingale dashboard can also embed a Grafana dashboard by URL.

Do I have to replace Prometheus?

No. Nightingale does not store time series. Prometheus keeps scraping and storing; Nightingale takes over rules, noise reduction and routing on top of it.

Can Alertmanager rules be migrated?

Rules, routes, silences and receivers each map onto a Nightingale object. The migration guide takes an alertmanager.yml apart entry by entry and lists the few that have no equivalent.

Can Nightingale read Zabbix data?

No. Moving from Zabbix is a rebuild: hosts become targets, templates become integrations, triggers become rules, and Categraf takes over collection. Zabbix never has to stop while you do it.

When should I not switch?

At moderate scale, with a GitOps-comfortable team and a rule count you can hold in your head, Prometheus + Alertmanager is enough. For network gear and SNMP-first estates, Zabbix is still home ground.

## Not sure? Run both.

Nightingale reads the storage you already have. Installing it changes nothing about the alerting you run today.

[Try live demo](http://43.106.19.165/api/n9e/auth/demo-login)[Install in 5 minutes](https://n9e.github.io/docs/get-started/quick-start.md)

# Connect Datadog Agent

Send Datadog Agent v1 metric series to Nightingale, with the API-version and authentication boundaries made explicit.

This page lets hosts with Datadog Agent keep their collectors and send **compatible metric series** to Nightingale.

Compatibility

Nightingale v9 registers `/datadog/api/v1/series`. It is not a complete Datadog backend and does not provide a v2 series receiver. The settings below are checked against **Datadog Agent 7.70.0**. Verify that other versions still support v1 before using them.

## Configure[​](#configure "Direct link to Configure")

Edit `/etc/datadog-agent/datadog.yaml` on Linux:

```
api_key: "replace-with-agent-key"

dd_url: "http://127.0.0.1:17000/datadog"

use_v2_api:

  series: false
```

Replace the URL and key. End `dd_url` at `/datadog`; the Agent appends the API path itself.

Changing `dd_url` alone is insufficient: [Agent 7.70.0 enables v2 series by default](https://github.com/DataDog/datadog-agent/blob/7.70.0/pkg/config/setup/config.go). Setting `use_v2_api.series: false` selects the v1 JSON format Nightingale receives.

Enable `[HTTP.APIForAgent].Enable` on the server. If `[HTTP.APIForAgent.BasicAuth]` is configured, Nightingale matches the request's `api_key` against its configured **password values**. A web-login token is not interchangeable with that key.

Without server authentication, Nightingale does not check this value, although the Agent still requires a valid nonempty configuration.

## Restart and verify[​](#verify "Direct link to Restart and verify")

```
sudo systemctl restart datadog-agent

sudo datadog-agent status

sudo journalctl -u datadog-agent -n 100 --no-pager
```

**Expected result**: the Agent starts and sends series to `/datadog/api/v1/series` without authentication or routing errors. In Nightingale's explorer, select the actual destination store and confirm that collected metrics appear and keep receiving new samples.

Nightingale replaces dots and hyphens in metric names with underscores: `system.cpu.user` becomes `system_cpu_user`. Inspect both Agent and Nightingale logs; a running service alone does not prove delivery.

Success on auxiliary compatibility endpoints does not prove that logs, APM, events or all service checks were stored. This guide covers the v1 metric-series path only. If your Agent cannot use it, choose [Categraf](https://n9e.github.io/docs/data/categraf/install.md) or a verified Prometheus collection path.

## Next[​](#next "Direct link to Next")

* [Data ingestion protocols](https://n9e.github.io/docs/reference/write-protocols.md)
* [Connected datasource with no data](https://n9e.github.io/docs/troubleshooting/no-data.md)

Implementation: [Pushgw routes](https://github.com/ccfos/nightingale/blob/01a8e22eb21d81f5cbe5c34e5a1511ff63e39983/pushgw/router/router.go) and [series parsing and authentication](https://github.com/ccfos/nightingale/blob/01a8e22eb21d81f5cbe5c34e5a1511ff63e39983/pushgw/router/router_datadog.go).

# Connect Telegraf

Send Telegraf metrics to Nightingale with HTTP output and Prometheus Remote Write, then verify the stored data.

By the end of this page, your existing Telegraf will write metrics to the store used by Nightingale. The example targets **Telegraf 1.36.3 and Nightingale v9**. Nightingale writes received metrics to its embedded TSDB or a configured external store.

## Before you start[​](#before-you-start "Direct link to Before you start")

* Nightingale is running and reachable from the Telegraf host on port 17000.
* `[HTTP.APIForAgent].Enable` is `true`.
* Choose the [embedded TSDB](https://n9e.github.io/docs/install/embedded-tsdb.md) or configure an [external writer](https://n9e.github.io/docs/install/external-tsdb.md).

Keep your existing Telegraf installation. For a new installation, use the [official instructions](https://docs.influxdata.com/telegraf/v1/install/) rather than the old 1.20.4 download script.

## Configure the output[​](#configure-output "Direct link to Configure the output")

Merge this into `telegraf.conf` and replace the URL. `outputs.http` is the output plugin; `prometheusremotewrite` is its serialization format.

```
[agent]

interval = "15s"

flush_interval = "15s"



[[outputs.http]]

url = "http://127.0.0.1:17000/prometheus/v1/write"

method = "POST"

data_format = "prometheusremotewrite"

[outputs.http.headers]

Content-Type = "application/x-protobuf"

Content-Encoding = "snappy"

X-Prometheus-Remote-Write-Version = "0.1.0"



[[inputs.cpu]]

percpu = false

totalcpu = true

collect_cpu_time = false

report_active = true



[[inputs.mem]]
```

If Nightingale configures `[HTTP.APIForAgent.BasicAuth]`, add matching `username` and `password` inside `[[outputs.http]]`, **before** its headers table. Leave them out when authentication is disabled.

Review any default InfluxDB output already enabled in the file; an unrelated failing output can obscure the result. OpenTSDB remains a compatibility protocol, but its metric names differ. Check existing dashboards when switching formats.

## Verify collection and delivery[​](#verify "Direct link to Verify collection and delivery")

```
telegraf --config /etc/telegraf/telegraf.conf --test

telegraf --config /etc/telegraf/telegraf.conf --once
```

**Expected result**: `--test` shows CPU and memory samples; `--once` performs collection and delivery without authentication, routing or connection errors. `--test` alone does not test delivery.

In Nightingale's metrics explorer, select the destination store and query `cpu_usage_active`. You should see series with Telegraf tags. Then restart the existing service. An installation with the official systemd unit can use `sudo systemctl restart telegraf`.

Telegraf does not send Categraf heartbeat metadata. Receiving metrics does not grant the same target-registration or self-healing capabilities. See the [1.36.3 format documentation](https://github.com/influxdata/telegraf/blob/v1.36.3/plugins/serializers/prometheusremotewrite/README.md) for Histogram and Summary batching limitations.

## Next[​](#next "Direct link to Next")

* [Data ingestion protocols](https://n9e.github.io/docs/reference/write-protocols.md)
* [Create your first alert](https://n9e.github.io/docs/alerting/first-rule.md)

# A2A endpoint

The A2A endpoint exposes Nightingale as an agent that other agent platforms can discover and call; the agent card declares the address and supported methods.

Where this page ends: a Nightingale agent that a third-party agent platform can discover and call on its own, plus one verified `message:send` request.

## Not the same thing as MCP[​](#not-the-same-thing-as-mcp "Direct link to Not the same thing as MCP")

|                          | `/mcp`                                                  | `/a2a`                                       |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| What the caller gets     | 74 fine-grained tools to orchestrate themselves         | One agent that talks                         |
| Interaction              | JSON-RPC tool calls                                     | Natural language in, natural language out    |
| Needs an LLM configured? | **No** — tools hit Nightingale's API directly           | **Yes** — it drives the built-in assistant   |
| Suits                    | Clients that bring their own model: Claude Code, Cursor | Somebody else's agent orchestration platform |

Both endpoints are on by default and share one auth path. **A question the assistant cannot answer in the UI, it cannot answer over A2A either** — get a conversation working first, see [Nightingale AI overview](https://n9e.github.io/docs/ai/nightingale-ai.md).

## The agent card is the only address a third party needs[​](#the-agent-card-is-the-only-address-a-third-party-needs "Direct link to The agent card is the only address a third party needs")

```
curl -s https://n9e.example.com/.well-known/agent-card.json
```

This address needs **no authentication** (the spec requires it to be discoverable). `/.well-known/agent.json` is an alias for older clients.

What the card declares:

| Field                                      | Value                                                                                  |
| ------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `name`                                     | `Nightingale Agent`                                                                    |
| `supportedInterfaces`                      | One HTTP+JSON interface at `<BaseURL>/a2a`                                             |
| `capabilities.streaming`                   | `true`                                                                                 |
| `defaultInputModes` / `defaultOutputModes` | Both `text`                                                                            |
| `securitySchemes`                          | `x-user-token` (apiKey, in a header); an extra `oidc` scheme appears when RSAuth is on |
| `skills`                                   | Every built-in skill, with its name, description and example prompts                   |

`skills` is generated from the built-in skills' frontmatter, so the caller sees what Nightingale is actually good at — diagnosing why a rule did not fire, analyzing a dashboard, generating PromQL — rather than one generic blurb.

An empty `BaseURL` is inferred from request headers. **Set it explicitly behind a reverse proxy**, or the third party may end up with an internal address:

```
[HTTP.A2A]

BaseURL = "https://n9e.example.com"
```

## Send a message[​](#send-a-message "Direct link to Send a message")

The REST binding path is `/a2a/message:send` (**no** `/v1` prefix). `messageId`, `role` and `parts` are all required, and the enum value for `role` is `ROLE_USER`:

```
curl -s -X POST https://n9e.example.com/a2a/message:send \

  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \

  -H 'X-User-Token: YOUR_TOKEN' \

  -d '{

    "message": {

      "messageId": "req-0001",

      "role": "ROLE_USER",

      "parts": [{ "text": "Which alerts are firing right now?" }]

    },

    "metadata": { "lang": "en_US" }

  }'
```

Expected result: a `task` object carrying `id`, `contextId`, `status.state`, and `n9e.chat_id` / `n9e.seq_id` under `metadata`. A `status.state` of `TASK_STATE_COMPLETED` means the turn finished; the answer is in `artifacts`. This step can take tens of seconds while the model thinks and calls tools — that is normal.

For multi-turn, put `"contextId": "<the contextId you got back>"` inside `message`. `contextId` maps one-to-one onto Nightingale's `chat_id`, which means an A2A conversation is the same conversation you see in the Nightingale AI conversation list.

## Which methods are supported[​](#which-methods-are-supported "Direct link to Which methods are supported")

| Method                      | Path                             |
| --------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| Send a message (unary)      | `POST /a2a/message:send`         |
| Send a message (SSE stream) | `POST /a2a/message:stream`       |
| Get a task                  | `GET /a2a/tasks/{id}`            |
| Cancel a task               | `POST /a2a/tasks/{id}:cancel`    |
| Resubscribe                 | `POST /a2a/tasks/{id}:subscribe` |

`tasks/list` is **deliberately not implemented** and returns `UnsupportedOperation` per the spec — enumerating tasks across users is meaningless for a built-in assistant and would leak other people's activity.

A bare GET on `/a2a` returns a short JSON hint listing the paths above. That exists so a client still using the legacy JSON-RPC style (`tasks/send`) gets a sentence it can read, rather than being redirected into the frontend SPA.

Task state lives in Redis with a 24-hour TTL, shared across instances. After it expires `tasks/get` returns task-not-found, but the conversation itself is still in the database.

## Reverse proxy and timeouts[​](#reverse-proxy-and-timeouts "Direct link to Reverse proxy and timeouts")

A2A sits at the root path and holds long connections:

```
location /.well-known/ {

    proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:17000;

}



location /a2a/ {

    proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:17000;

    proxy_http_version 1.1;

    proxy_set_header Host $host;



    proxy_buffering off;        # without this, streaming answers never emit anything

    proxy_read_timeout 3600s;   # the default 60s cuts answers in half

    proxy_send_timeout 3600s;

}
```

The server sends an empty "working" status heartbeat every 30 seconds precisely to survive gateway idle timeouts — but the gateway's own read timeout still has to be raised.

## The command-line client[​](#the-command-line-client "Direct link to The command-line client")

The repository ships a test client built on the official SDK:

```
go run ./cmd/a2a-cli --server http://127.0.0.1:17000 --token YOUR_TOKEN \

    --message "Show the alert events currently firing"



# Continue the same conversation

go run ./cmd/a2a-cli --server http://127.0.0.1:17000 --token YOUR_TOKEN \

    --context-id CHAT_ID --message "Analyze the first one in more detail"
```

It streams by default; `--get` calls `tasks/get` afterwards to prove the task really was stored.

## Turning it off[​](#turning-it-off "Direct link to Turning it off")

```
[HTTP.A2A]

Disable = true   # closes /a2a, /mcp and the agent card together
```

To close MCP only and keep A2A, use `DisableMCP = true`.

* Get the assistant answering first: [Nightingale AI overview](https://n9e.github.io/docs/ai/nightingale-ai.md)
* Let callers use their own accounts: [OAuth 2.1 and external identity providers](https://n9e.github.io/docs/ai/oauth.md)

# Agents and conversation history

Conversation history is stored server-side and can be reviewed or deleted; in the open-source build an agent is an internal binding, not something you create.

Two separate things share this page, and they are worth telling apart up front. **Conversation history is a real, everyday feature.** **"Agent" is an internal binding in the open-source build, not something you create** — the details are in the second half so you do not go looking for a page that is not there.

## Where conversations live[​](#where-conversations-live "Direct link to Where conversations live")

Every turn is written to the database as it happens, so a conversation survives a page reload, a different browser and a restart of `n9e`. Two tables hold it:

| Table                  | What it holds                                                                    |
| ---------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ai_assistant_chat`    | One row per conversation: its id, its owner, its title, when it was last touched |
| `ai_assistant_message` | One row per turn: your question, the answer, and the tool calls behind it        |

Both bodies are compressed, so the rows are smaller than the transcripts suggest.

**Conversations are strictly per user.** Every read and write checks that the requesting account owns the conversation, with no administrator override, so one person's chats are not visible to anyone else — including through the API.

An `/a2a` conversation is the same object: the `contextId` a caller passes back is the `chat_id`, so an agent talking to Nightingale through [A2A](https://n9e.github.io/docs/ai/a2a.md) appears in that user's list alongside what they typed in the browser.

## What you can do with one[​](#what-you-can-do-with-one "Direct link to What you can do with one")

The **Conversations** section of the Nightingale AI sidebar lists yours, newest first, grouped into Today / Yesterday / older, with a box that filters on title. Hovering a row reveals a menu:

* **Rename** — inline. Titles are generated from the first question otherwise, and renaming pins yours so the automatic title never overwrites it;
* **Share** — copies a link that opens the conversation read-only. The server still checks ownership on every read, so **the link works for you and nobody else**; treat it as a bookmark to a read-only view, not as a way to hand a transcript to a colleague. To do that, copy the text.

## Deleting one[​](#deleting-one "Direct link to Deleting one")

**There is no delete button.** The endpoint exists; nothing in the interface calls it. Until that changes, deleting is an API call with your own token:

```
curl -s --request DELETE \

  -H 'X-User-Token: YOUR_TOKEN' \

  http://127.0.0.1:17000/api/n9e/assistant/chat/YOUR_CHAT_ID
```

The chat id is the last path segment of the conversation's URL. Deleting removes its messages as well, and — the ownership check again — only works on your own conversations.

**There is no retention policy and no TTL.** Nothing expires conversations, so on a busy instance these two tables only grow. If that matters, script the call above; they are also ordinary tables that your backup and archival routine can treat like any other.

## What an "agent" is here[​](#what-an-agent-is-here "Direct link to What an \"agent\" is here")

There is an `ai_agent` table, and rows in it bind a **use case** to an LLM config and a list of skills. In the open-source build that is much less than it sounds:

* **The only use case is `chat`**, and exactly one enabled row for it is ever consulted;
* **A row is created for you at startup** — `default-chat-agent`, bound to no specific model — so the assistant works out of the box;
* **There is no system prompt and no tool selection on the row.** Both are compiled into the product; nothing on an agent changes how the assistant thinks or what it may call;
* **The skills bound to the chat agent are ignored** on the ordinary conversation path. Skills are discovered from the catalogue and loaded on demand instead — see [Install, manage and write Skills](https://n9e.github.io/docs/ai/skills.md);
* **There is no menu entry**, no permission point of its own, and the list page that does exist has had its create button removed. It is administrator-only and reachable by typing the address.

So: do not build a workflow on named agents in the open-source build. If a page or a screenshot elsewhere shows agent management as a feature, it is not this edition.

## What to change instead of an agent[​](#what-to-change-instead-of-an-agent "Direct link to What to change instead of an agent")

| What you actually want                      | Where to do it                                                                                                                                               |
| ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| A different model for the assistant         | Mark a different LLM config **Default** — it wins over any agent binding anyway ([Configure an LLM provider](https://n9e.github.io/docs/ai/llm-provider.md)) |
| Different behaviour for a class of question | Write a skill; its description decides when it applies ([Install, manage and write Skills](https://n9e.github.io/docs/ai/skills.md))                         |
| More tools for one procedure                | `builtin_tools` in that skill's frontmatter                                                                                                                  |
| A longer diagnostic chain                   | `max_iterations` in that skill's frontmatter                                                                                                                 |
| Restrict what the assistant can reach       | The asking account's role and business groups ([Permission inheritance and RBAC](https://n9e.github.io/docs/ai/permissions.md))                              |

## Next[​](#next "Direct link to Next")

* What the assistant does with a conversation: [Nightingale AI overview](https://n9e.github.io/docs/ai/nightingale-ai.md)
* The skill mechanism that replaces per-agent prompts: [Install, manage and write Skills](https://n9e.github.io/docs/ai/skills.md)
* Conversations that arrive from another agent: [A2A endpoint](https://n9e.github.io/docs/ai/a2a.md)

# Safe automation patterns

Safe AI automation keeps a person in the loop at write time: the assistant proposes and you confirm, one account can write, or AI drafts a script that a human runs.

This page is about one boundary: how much you let an AI change, and what stops a wrong change from becoming an outage. The short answer is that the safe patterns are the ones where a person is still in the loop at the moment of the write — and Nightingale enforces that on one surface and leaves it to you on the others.

## Three surfaces, three write postures[​](#three-surfaces-three-write-postures "Direct link to Three surfaces, three write postures")

| Surface            | Can it write?                      | What stands between the model and the database                                             |
| ------------------ | ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Built-in assistant | Yes, a short list                  | A server-side confirmation card on every update; a form when a create is missing something |
| `/mcp`             | Only after you turn write tools on | Nothing at call time — a write tool writes on the first call                               |
| `/a2a`             | It is the built-in assistant       | Same confirmation, but the confirming turn has to come from the calling agent              |

One property they share, and it is worth stating plainly: **there is no delete tool anywhere.** Not in the assistant's toolbox, not among the MCP tools. The worst an AI can do to a rule, a dashboard or a user is change it — which is why "who changed this" matters more here than "who deleted it".

## Pattern 1 — the assistant proposes, you confirm[​](#pattern-1--the-assistant-proposes-you-confirm "Direct link to Pattern 1 — the assistant proposes, you confirm")

This is the default and the one to prefer, because the gate is in the server rather than in a prompt somebody can talk their way around.

The tools it covers are the ones that modify something that already exists — an alert rule, a dashboard, a muting rule, a notification rule, a subscription — plus skill authoring. Each works in two legs:

1. **Propose.** The tool computes the change, stores it under a one-time id, and returns **without writing**. The turn ends with a card listing what would change, written by the tool itself so the model cannot soften it.
2. **Confirm.** Only your reply in a **later turn** applies it, replayed from what was stored. The model is not consulted again, so it cannot quietly alter the payload between showing you the diff and writing it.

Three things bound a proposal, all deliberate:

* it expires after **30 minutes**;
* it can be confirmed **once** — a second confirmation finds nothing to apply;
* the object's state is fingerprinted at propose time, and a confirmation is **refused if somebody edited it in the meantime** rather than overwriting their work.

Creates are handled differently but with the same intent: when a create tool is missing something it must not guess — a business group, a team — it does not choose one. It returns a dropdown and waits for you.

## Pattern 2 — read-only by default, one account that can write[​](#pattern-2--read-only-by-default-one-account-that-can-write "Direct link to Pattern 2 — read-only by default, one account that can write")

On `/mcp` there is no confirmation card, so the boundary has to be built out of accounts and config. The pattern that works:

* every client gets its own least-privilege account and its own token, so an incident is traceable to one integration ([Personal token authentication](https://n9e.github.io/docs/ai/token-auth.md));
* write tools stay off unless one specific client genuinely needs them, and even then the toolsets are narrowed to what that client does — with `users` and `roles` dropped ([Enable write tools safely](https://n9e.github.io/docs/ai/write-tools.md));
* the account's business-group membership is the real limit on blast radius, because it applies to reads and writes alike ([Permission inheritance and RBAC](https://n9e.github.io/docs/ai/permissions.md)).

If what you actually wanted was "let the AI help me change configuration", note that the built-in assistant already does that with a confirmation step. Turning MCP write tools on to get the same outcome trades that away.

## Pattern 3 — the AI drafts the script, a person runs it[​](#pattern-3--the-ai-drafts-the-script-a-person-runs-it "Direct link to Pattern 3 — the AI drafts the script, a person runs it")

Self-healing is the case where automation is most tempting and most dangerous, so it is worth being precise about what the open-source build does.

**The assistant can read your self-healing scripts and write new ones as text.** It has read access to the script library, and a built-in skill for authoring them:

> Write a self-healing script for disk cleanup

> How does a self-healing script read alert fields from stdin?

**It cannot create one and it cannot run one.** There is no tool for either. Saving the script and running it against hosts stays entirely in **Alerts & Notifications → Self-healing**, where the existing controls apply — see [Trigger self-healing with ibex / webhook](https://n9e.github.io/docs/events/self-healing.md).

That division is the pattern: the model produces a proposal in a form you can read and review, a human commits it, and the execution path never has a model in it.

## Guardrails worth setting deliberately[​](#guardrails-worth-setting-deliberately "Direct link to Guardrails worth setting deliberately")

| Guardrail                                                        | Where                                                                                                                        |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Write tools off on `/mcp` — the default; leave it                | `MCPEnableWriteTools` under `[HTTP.A2A]`                                                                                     |
| Drop `users` and `roles` from any client that does write         | `MCPToolsets`                                                                                                                |
| Drop `logs` if you have SQL datasources registered               | `MCPToolsets`, and see [Permission inheritance and RBAC](https://n9e.github.io/docs/ai/permissions.md)                       |
| Refuse skill scripts rather than running them unisolated         | `RequireIsolation` under `[Center.Sandbox]`, see [Install, manage and write Skills](https://n9e.github.io/docs/ai/skills.md) |
| Keep the AI account out of business groups it has no business in | **Organization → Teams**                                                                                                     |
| Never give an AI account the `Admin` role                        | It bypasses the business-group layer entirely                                                                                |

## How to check what changed[​](#how-to-check-what-changed "Direct link to How to check what changed")

Three trails, in increasing order of effort:

**The object itself.** Anything changed through the assistant or over MCP carries the acting user's name in its "updated by" field, exactly as a UI edit would. The list pages show it.

**The conversation.** An assistant change leaves the proposal card and your confirmation in the transcript, which is stored per user and not expired — so "what exactly did I approve" is answerable months later. See [Agents and conversation history](https://n9e.github.io/docs/ai/agents.md).

**The logs.** Every `/mcp` request is logged with the tool name, arguments and the acting user; every skill script execution is logged with its isolation level and exit code. Details and a grep-able example are in [Enable write tools safely](https://n9e.github.io/docs/ai/write-tools.md).

## What it will not do on its own[​](#what-it-will-not-do-on-its-own "Direct link to What it will not do on its own")

In the open-source build **every AI action starts with a person in a conversation**. Nothing is scheduled, nothing runs unattended, and no tool executes a command on a monitored host. A skill script is the one thing that runs code, it only runs when the model calls it inside a turn you started, and you can refuse it outright — again, in [Install, manage and write Skills](https://n9e.github.io/docs/ai/skills.md).

## Next[​](#next "Direct link to Next")

* The confirmation mechanism in context: [Nightingale AI overview](https://n9e.github.io/docs/ai/nightingale-ai.md)
* The MCP write switch: [Enable write tools safely](https://n9e.github.io/docs/ai/write-tools.md)
* Prompts that keep a session read-only: [Common investigation workflows](https://n9e.github.io/docs/ai/workflows.md)
